items.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I played second guitar behind Curtis Mayfield

ctx.x: I taught a course at Vanderbilt for eight years, it’s called Rhythm & Blues Tore Down the Walls of Segregation. I’m teaching it now at Virginia/Wesleyan in Virginia Beach where

I live now. I taught it at Vanderbilt for eight years. But yeah, very passionate about that. Because I lived through it in the 60s. My band in Richmond, we became a really popular back-up band for black artists. Back then there were very few artists that carried bands. James Brown had his big 18 piece band and they were like a machine. I get chills just thinking about that, when I first saw that 18 piece, that curtain open up and those guys are in tuxedos. You know. Three drummers, two guitarists, bass player, an…

items.title: Buckingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2019
items.q: like the Impressions he was talking about, Curtis Mayfield and

ctx.x: Yesterday in your film compilation, I don’t know if Andrew Young said this or if you inserted this. But I believe it was like, “The music comes first and the lyrics” —

That was Andrew Young. That’s when he made the statement about you could say that music was more successful than the courts in integrating society. He said people would be singing along with it, like the Impressions he was talking about, Curtis Mayfield and

the Impressions. He said and it’s only until later you realize what you’re singing, the lyric, and what you’re singing about. You’re singing along and then later, whoa. You know, “People get ready there’s a train” — we’re talking about the movement, the Civil Rights Movement here. Yeah. That was Andrew Young.
